esurient: Inclined to eat; hungry; voracious. Bailey. "Poor, but esurient." Carlyle. | One who is hungry or greedy. An insatiable esurient after riches. Wood.
espringal: An engine of war used for throwing viretons, large stones, and other missiles; a springal.
esloin: To remove; to banish; to withdraw; to avoid; to eloign. (old) From worldly cares he did himself esloin. Spenser.
essoin: 1. (Eng. Law) An excuse for not appearing in court at the return of process; the allegation of an excuse to the court. 2. Excuse; exemption. (old) From every work he challenged essoin. Spenser. | To excuse for nonappearance in court. "I 'll not essoin thee." Quarles.
escribed: Drawn outside of; -- used to designate a circle that touches one of the sides of a given triangle, and also the other two sides produced.
escharine: Like, or pertaining to, the genus Eschara, or family Escharidæ.
escritorial: Of or pertaining to an escritoire.
estafet: A courier who conveys messages to another courier; a military courier sent from one part of an army to another.
estrange: 1. To withdraw; to withhold; hence, reflexively, to keep at a distance; to cease to be familiar and friendly with. We must estrange our belief from everything which is not clearly and distinctly evidenced. Glanvill. Had we . . . estranged ourselves from them in things indifferent. Hooker. 2. To divert from its original use or purpose, or from its former possessor; to alienate.
esophagus: That part of the alimentary canal between the pharynx and the stomach; the gullet. See Illust. of Digestive apparatus, under Digestive. [Written also .]
esthesiometer: An instrument to measure the degree of sensation, by determining at how short a distance two impressions upon the skin can be distinguished, and thus to determine whether the condition of tactile sensibility is normal or altered.
esculin: A glucoside obtained from the Æsculus hippocastanum, or horse- chestnut, and characterized by its fine blue fluorescent solutions. [Written also æsculin.]
escarpment: A steep descent or declivity; steep face or edge of a ridge; ground about a fortified place, cut away nearly vertically to prevent hostile approach. See Scarp.
espinel: A kind of ruby. See Spinel.
ess: A suffix used to form feminine nouns; as, actress, deaconess, songstress.
escent: A suffix signifying beginning, beginning to be; as, adolescent, effervescent, etc.
estimableness: The quality of deserving esteem or regard.
essorant: Standing, but with the wings spread, as if about to fly; -- said of a bird borne as a charge on an escutcheon.
eschatology: The doctrine of the last or final things, as death, judgment, and the events therewith connected.
esquire: Originally, a shield-bearer or armor-bearer, an attendant on a knight; in modern times, a title of dignity next in degree below knight and above gentleman; also, a title of office and courtesy; | To wait on as an esquire or attendant in public; to attend. [Colloq.]
espionage: The practice or employment of spies; the practice of watching the words and conduct of others, to make discoveries, as spies or secret emissaries; secret watching.
escalade: A furious attack made by troops on a fortified place, in which ladders are used to pass a ditch or mount a rampart. Sin enters, not by escalade, but by cunning or treachery. Buckminster. | To mount and pass or enter by means of ladders; to scale; as, to escalate a wall.
esox: A genus of fresh-water fishes, including pike and pickerel.
escheat: 1. (Law) (a) (Feud. & Eng. Law) The falling back or reversion of lands, by some casualty or accident, to the lord of the fee, in consequence of the extinction of the blood of the tenant, which may… | To revert, or become forfeited, to the lord, the crown, or the State, as lands by the failure of persons entitled to hold the same, or by forfeiture. Note: In this country it is the general rule that…
escambio: A license formerly required for the making over a bill of exchange to another over sea. Cowell.
estreat: A true copy, duplicate, or extract of an original writing or record, esp. of amercements or penalties set down in the rolls of court to be levied by the bailiff, or other officer. Cowell. | (a) To extract or take out from the records of a court, and send up to the court of exchequer to be enforced; -- said of a forfeited recognizance. (b) To bring in to the exchequer, as a fine.
estafette: A courier who conveys messages to another courier; a military courier sent from one part of an army to another.
escheator: An officer whose duty it is to observe what escheats have taken place, and to take charge of them. Burrill.
espial: 1. The act of espying; notice; discovery. Screened from espial by the jutting cape. Byron. 2. One who espies; a spy; a scout. (old) "Their espials . . . brought word." Holland.
escaloped: 1. Cut or marked in the form of an escalop; scalloped. 2. (Her.) Covered with a pattern resembling a series of escalop shells, each of which issues from between two others. Its appearance is that of a surface covered with scales. Escaloped oysters (Cookery). See under Scalloped.
escalator: A stairway or incline arranged like an endless belt so that the steps or treads ascend or descend continuously, and one stepping upon it is carried up or down; -- a trade term.
esopian: Of or pertaining to Æsop, or in his manner.
estuary: 1. A place where water boils up; a spring that wells forth. (old) Boyle. 2. A passage, as the mouth of a river or lake, where the tide meets the current; an arm of the sea; a frith. | Belonging to, or formed in, an estuary; as, estuary strata. Lyell.
escroll: 1. A scroll. (old) 2. (Her.) (a) A long strip or scroll resembling a ribbon or a band of parchment, or the like, anciently placed above the shield, and supporting the crest. (b) In modern heraldry, a similar ribbon on which the motto is inscribed.
escheatage: The right of succeeding to an escheat. Sherwood.
ester: An ethereal salt, or compound ether, consisting of an organic radical united with the residue of any oxygen acid, organic or inorganic; thus the natural fats are esters of glycerin and the fatty acids, oleic, etc.
estimable: 1. Capable of being estimated or valued; as, estimable damage. Paley. . 2. Valuable; worth a great price. A pound of man's flesh, taken from a man, Is not so estimable, profitable neither, As flesh… | A thing worthy of regard. One of the peculiar estimables of her country. Sir T. Browne.
esculent: Suitable to be used by man for food; eatable; edible; as, esculent plants; esculent fish. Esculent grain for food. Sir W. Jones. Esculent swallow (Zoöl.), the swallow which makes the edible bird's-… | Anything that is fit for eating; that which may be safely eaten by man.
essence: 1. The constituent elementary notions which constitute a complex notion, and must be enumerated to define it; sometimes called the nominal essence. 2. The constituent quality or qualities which… | To perfume; to scent. "Essenced fops." Addison.
eschara: A genus of Bryozoa which produce delicate corals, often incrusting like lichens, but sometimes branched.
essenism: The doctrine or the practices of the Essenes. De Quincey.
escrow: A deed, bond, or other written engagement, delivered to a third person, to be held by him till some act is done or some condition is performed, and then to be by him delivered to the grantee. Blackstone.
eschatological: Pertaining to the last or final things.
esthetical: Same as Æsthete, Æsthetic, Æsthetical, Æsthetics, etc.
esplanade: 1. (Fort.) (a) A clear space between a citadel and the nearest houses of the town. Campbell (Mil. Dict. ). (b) The glacis of the counterscarp, or the slope of the parapet of the covered way toward the country. 2. (Hort.) A grass plat; a lawn. Simmonds. 3. Any clear, level space used for public walks or drives; esp., a terrace by the seaside.
eschevin: The alderman or chief officer of an ancient guild. (old)
estate: 1. Settled condition or form of existence; state; condition or circumstances of life or of any person; situation. "When I came to man's estate." Shak. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of… | 1. To establish. (old) Beau. & Fl. 2. Tom settle as a fortune. (old) Shak. 3. To endow with an estate. (old) Then would I . . . Estate them with large land and territory. Tennyson.
esperanto: An artificial language, intended to be universal, devised by Dr. Zamenhof, a Russian, who adopted the pseudonym "Dr. Esperanto" in publishing his first pamphlet regarding it in 1887. The vocabulary is very largely based upon words common to the chief European languages, and sounds peculiar to any one language are eliminated.
espouse: 1. To betroth; to promise in marriage; to give as spouse. A virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph. Luke i. 27. 2. To take as spouse; to take to wife; to marry. Lavinia will I make my empress, . . . And in the sacred Pantheon her espouse. Shak. 3. To take to one's self with a view to maintain; to make one's own; to take up the cause of; to adopt; to embrace.
esquisse: The first sketch of a picture or model of a statue.
estoppel: (a) A stop; an obstruction or bar to one's alleging or denying a fact contrary to his own previous action, allegation, or denial; an admission, by words or conduct, which induces another to purchase rights, against which the party making such admission can not take a position inconsistent with the admission.
estoile: A six-pointed star whose rays are wavy, instead of straight like those of a mullet. [Written also étoile.] Estoile of eight points, a star which has four straight and four wavy rays. -- Estoile of four points. Same as Cross estoilé, under Cross.
essentiate: To form or constitute the essence or being of. (old) Boyle. | To become assimilated; to be changed into the essence. (old) B. Jonson.
estrich: 1. Ostrich. (old) Massinger. 2. (Com.) The down of the ostrich. Brande & C.
espauliere: A defense for the shoulder, composed of flexible overlapping plates of metal, used in the 15th century; -- the origin of the modern epaulette. Fairholt.
essentially: In an essential manner or degree; in an indispensable degree; really; as, essentially different.
estimation: 1. The act of estimating. Shak. 2. An opinion or judgment of the worth, extent, or quantity of anything, formed without using precise data; valuation; as, estimations of distance, magnitude, amount, or moral qualities. If he be poorer that thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest, and the priest shall value him. Lev. xxvii. 8. 3.
essonite: Cinnamon stone, a variety of garnet. See Garnet.
esophagotomy: The operation of making an incision into the esophagus, for the purpose of removing any foreign substance that obstructs the passage. [Written also oesophagotomy.]
estop: To impede or bar by estoppel. A party will be estopped by his admissions, where his intent is to influence another, or derive an advantage to himself. Abbott.
espalier: A railing or trellis upon which fruit trees or shrubs are trained, as upon a wall; a tree or row of trees so trained. And figs from standard and espalier join. Pope. | To form an espalier of, or to protect by an espalier.
estramacon: 1. A straight, heavy sword with two edges, used in the 16th and 17th centuries. 2. A blow with edge of a sword. Farrow.
essene: One of a sect among the Jews in the time of our Savior, remarkable for their strictness and abstinence.
estrepement: A destructive kind of waste, committed by a tenant for life, in lands, woods, or houses. Cowell.
espadon: A long, heavy, two-handed and two-edged sword, formerly used by Spanish foot soldiers and by executioners. Wilhelm.
escopet: A kind of firearm; a carbine.
essayist: A writer of an essay, or of essays. B. Jonson.
establishedsuit: A plain suit in which a player (or side) could, except for trumping, take tricks with all his remaining cards.
espousement: The act of espousing, or the state of being espoused.
eskimo: One of a peculiar race inhabiting Arctic America and Greenland. In many respects the Eskimos resemble the Mongolian race. [Written also Esquimau.] Eskimo dog (Zoöl.), one of breed of large and powerful dogs used by the Eskimos to draw sledges. It closely resembles the gray wolf, with which it is often crossed.
estancia: A grazing; a country house. [Spanish America]
estovers: Necessaries or supples; an allowance to a person out of an estate or other thing for support; as of wood to a tenant for life, etc., of sustenance to a man confined for felony of his estate, or alimony to a woman divorced out of her husband's estate. Blackstone. Common of estovers. See under Common, n.
estaminet: A café, or room in a café, in which smoking is allowed.
esparto: A species of Spanish grass (Macrochloa tenacissima), of which cordage, shoes, baskets, etc., are made. It is also used for making paper.
escot: To pay the reckoning for; to support; to maintain. (old) Shak.
esque: A suffix of certain words from the French, Italian, and Spanish. It denotes manner or style; like; as, arabesque, after the manner of the Arabs.
eschynite: A rare mineral, containing chiefly niobium, titanium, thorium, and cerium. It was so called by Berzelius on account of the inability of chemical science, at the time of its discovery, to separate some of its constituents.
esteemer: One who esteems; one who sets a high value on any thing. The proudest esteemer of his own parts. Locke.
estre: The inward part of a building; the interior. (old) Chaucer.
estrepe: To strip or lay bare, as land of wood, houses, etc.; to commit waste.
esparcet: The common sainfoin (Onobrychis sativa), an Old World leguminous forage plant.
escopette: A kind of firearm; a carbine.
escutcheoned: Having an escutcheon; furnished with a coat of arms or ensign. Young.
estimative: 1. Inclined, or able, to estimate; serving for, or capable of being used in, estimating. We find in animals an estimative or judicial faculty. Sir M. Hale. 2. Pertaining to an estimate.
est: A suffix used to form the superlative of adjectives and adverbs; as, smoothest; earl(y)iest.
estrade: A portion of the floor of a room raised above the general level, as a place for a bed or a throne; a platform; a dais. He [the teacher] himself should have his desk on a mounted estrade or platform. J. G. Fitch.
escarp: The side of the ditch next the parapet; -- same as scarp, and opposed to counterscarp. | To make into, or furnish with, a steep slope, like that of a scrap. Carleton.
escape: 1. To flee from and avoid; to be saved or exempt from; to shun; to obtain security from; as, to escape danger. "Sailors that escaped the wreck." Shak. 2. To avoid the notice of; | 1. To flee, and become secure from danger; -- often followed by from or out of. Haste, for thy life escape, nor look behindKeble. 2. To get clear from danger or evil of any form;
esurine: Causing hunger; eating; corroding. (old) Wiseman. | A medicine which provokes appetites, or causes hunger. (old)
estrangedness: State of being estranged; estrangement. Prynne.
esprit: Spirit. Esprit de corps (, a French phrase much used by English writers to denote the common spirit pervading the members of a body or association of persons. It implies sympathy, enthusiasm, devotion, and jealous regard for the honor of the body as a whole.
esoterics: Mysterious or hidden doctrines; secret science.
esodic: Conveying impressions from the surface of the body to the spinal cord; -- said of certain nerves. Opposed to exodic.
esotery: Mystery; esoterics; -- opposed to exotery. A. Tucker.
espousal: 1. The act of espousing or betrothing; especially, in the plural, betrothal; plighting of the troths; a contract of marriage; sometimes, the marriage ceremony. 2. The uniting or allying one's self with anything; maintenance; adoption; as, the espousal of a quarrel. The open espousal of his cause. Lord Orford.
escalop: 1. (Zoöl.) A bivalve shell of the genus Pecten. See Scallop. 2. A regular, curving indenture in the margin of anything. See Scallop. "So many jags or escalops." Ray. 3. (a) The figure or shell of an escalop, considered as a sign that the bearer had been on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. Hence: (b) (Her.) A bearing or a charge consisting of an escalop shell.
establishmentarian: One who regards the Church primarily as an establishment formed by the State, and overlooks its intrinsic spiritual character. Shipley.
esopic: Same as Æsopian. | Same as Æsopian, Æsopic.
essentiality: The quality of being essential; the essential part. Jer. Taylor.
escuage: Service of the shield, a species of knight service by which a tenant was bound to follow his lord to war, at his own charge. It was afterward exchanged for a pecuniary satisfaction. Called also scutage. Blackstone.
esteem: 1. To set a value on; to appreciate the worth of; to estimate; to value; to reckon. Then he forsook God, which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation. Deut. xxxii. 15. | To form an estimate; to have regard to the value; to consider. (old) We ourselves esteem not of that obedience, or love, or gift, which is of force. Milton.
esemplastic: Shaped into one; tending to, or formative into, unity. Coleridge.
essoign: 1. (Eng. Law) An excuse for not appearing in court at the return of process; the allegation of an excuse to the court. 2. Excuse; exemption. (old) From every work he challenged essoin. Spenser. Essoin day (Eng. Law), the first general return day of the term, on which the court sits to receive essoins. Blackstone.
eschew: 1. To shun; to avoid, as something wrong, or from a feeling of distaste; to keep one's self clear of. They must not only eschew evil, but do good. Bp. Beveridge. 2. To escape from; to avoid. (old) He who obeys, destruction shall eschew. Sandys.
estrangement: The act of estranging, or the state of being estranged; alienation. An estrangement from God. J. C. Shairp. A long estrangement from better things. South.
esoteric: Designed for, and understood by, the specially initiated alone; not communicated, or not intelligible, to the general body of followers; private; interior; acroamatic; -- said of the private and more recondite instructions and doctrines of philosophers. Opposed to exoteric.
esplees: The full profits or products which ground or land yields, as the hay of the meadows, the feed of the pasture, the grain of arable fields, the rents, services, and the like. Cowell.
estuation: The act of estuating; commotion, as of a fluid; agitation. The estuations of joys and fears. W. Montagu.
estacade: A dike of piles in the sea, a river, etc., to check the approach of an enemy.
estimate: 1. To judge and form an opinion of the value of, from imperfect data, -- either the extrinsic (money), or intrinsic (moral), value; to fix the worth of roughly or in a general way; | A valuing or rating by the mind, without actually measuring, weighing, or the like; rough or approximate calculation; as, an estimate of the cost of a building, or of the quantity of water in a pond.
eschscholtzia: A genus of papaveraceous plants, found in California and upon the west coast of North America, some species of which produce beautiful yellow, orange, rose-colored, or white flowers; the California poppy.
essential: 1. Belonging to the essence, or that which makes an object, or class of objects, what it is. Majestic as the voice sometimes became, there was forever in it an essential character of plaintiveness. | 1. Existence; being. (old) Milton. 2. That which is essential; first or constituent principle; as, the essentials or religion.
escapade: 1. The fling of a horse, or ordinary kicking back of his heels; a gambol. 2. Act by which one breaks loose from the rules of propriety or good sense; a freak; a prank. Carlyle.
especially: In an especial manner; chiefly; particularly; peculiarly; in an uncommon degree.
escort: 1. A body of armed men to attend a person of distinction for the sake of affording safety when on a journey; one who conducts some one as an attendant; a guard, as of prisoners on a march; | To attend with a view to guard and protect; to accompany as safeguard; to give honorable or ceremonious attendance to; -- used esp. with reference to journeys or excursions on land;
establish: 1. To make stable or firm; to fix immovably or firmly; to set (a thing) in a place and make it stable there; to settle; to confirm. So were the churches established in the faith. Acts xvi. 5. The best established tempers can scarcely forbear being borne down. Burke. Confidence which must precede union could be established only by consummate prudence and self-control. Bancroft.
escutcheon: 1. (Her.) The surface, usually a shield, upon which bearings are marshaled and displayed. The surface of the escutcheon is called the field, the upper part is called the chief, and the lower part the base (see Chiff, and Field.). That side of the escutcheon which is on the right hand of the knight who bears the shield on his arm is called dexter, and the other side sinister.
escurial: A palace and mausoleum of the kinds of Spain, being a vast and wonderful structure about twenty-five miles northwest of Madrid. Note: The ground plan is said to be in the form of a gridiron, the structure being designed in honor of St. Lawrence, who suffered martyrdom by being broiled on gridiron; but the resemblance is very slight.
escrol: 1. A scroll. (old) 2. (Her.) (a) A long strip or scroll resembling a ribbon or a band of parchment, or the like, anciently placed above the shield, and supporting the crest. (b) In modern heraldry, a similar ribbon on which the motto is inscribed.
establishment: 1. The act of establishing; a ratifying or ordaining; settlement; confirmation. 2. The state of being established, founded, and the like; fixed state. 3. That which is established; as: (a) A form of government, civil or ecclesiastical; especially, a system of religion maintained by the civil power; as, the Episcopal establishment of England.
esthetic: Same as Æsthete, Æsthetic, Æsthetical, Æsthetics, etc.
escapement: 1. The act of escaping; escape. 2. Way of escape; vent. An escapement for youthful high spirits. G. Eliot. 3. The contrivance in a timepiece which connects the train of wheel work with the pendulum or balance, giving to the latter the impulse by which it is kept in vibration; -- so called because it allows a tooth to escape from a pallet at each vibration.
esnecy: A prerogative given to the eldest coparcener to choose first after an inheritance is divide. Mozley & W.
estuate: To boil up; to swell and rage; to be agitated. Bacon.
estray: Any valuable animal, not wild, found wandering from its owner; a stray. Burrill.
estimator: One who estimates or values; a valuer. Jer. Taylor.
esthete: Same as Æsthete, Æsthetic, Æsthetical, Æsthetics, etc.
esteemable: Worthy of esteem; estimable. "Esteemable qualities." Pope.
especial: Distinguished among others of the same class or kind; special; concerning a species or a single object; principal; particular; as, in an especial manner or degree. Syn. -- Peculiar; special; particular; uncommon; chief. See Peculiar.
estrapade: The action of a horse, when, to get rid of his rider, he rears, plunges, and kicks furiously.
espouser: One who espouses; one who embraces the cause of another or makes it his own.
eschar: A dry slough, crust, or scab, which separates from the healthy part of the body, as that produced by a burn, or the application of caustics. | In Ireland, one of the continuous mounds or ridges of gravelly and sandy drift which extend for many miles over the surface of the country. Similar ridges in Scotland are called kames or kams.
escharotic: Serving or tending to form an eschar;; producing a scar; caustic. | A substance which produces an eschar; a caustic, esp., a mild caustic.
espy: 1. To catch sight of; to perceive with the eyes; to discover, as a distant object partly concealed, or not obvious to notice; to see at a glance; to discern unexpectedly; to spy; as, to espy land; | To look or search narrowly; to look about; to watch; to take notice; to spy. Stand by the way, and espy. Jer. xlviii. 19.
esculic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, the horse-chestnut; as, esculic acid.
estufa: An assembly room in dwelling of the Pueblo Indians. L. H. Morgan.
esthetics: The theory or philosophy of taste; the science of the beautiful in nature and art; esp. that which treats of the expression and embodiment of beauty by art. | Same as Æsthete, Æsthetic, Æsthetical, Æsthetics, etc.
essay: 1. An effort made, or exertion of body or mind, for the performance of anything; a trial; attempt; as, to make an essay to benefit a friend. "The essay at organization." M. Arnold. 2. | 1. To exert one's power or faculties upon; to make an effort to perform; to attempt; to endeavor; to make experiment or trial of; to try. What marvel if I thus essay to sing Byron.
esquimau: Same as Eskimo. It is . . . an error to suppose that where an Esquimau can live, a civilized man can live also. McClintock.
essoiner: An attorney who sufficiently excuses the absence of another.
eserine: An alkaloid found in the Calabar bean, and the seed of Physostigma venenosum; physostigmine. It is used in ophthalmic surgery for its effect in contracting the pupil.
escritoire: A piece of furniture used as a writing table, commonly with drawers, pigeonholes, and the like; a secretary or writing desk.
